newsitem.title: USA: Banks outsourcing proprietary trading to CTAs.
newsitem.headline: Banks outsourcing proprietary trading to CTAs.

text.p: Some banks are starting to outsource proprietary trading to commodity trading advisers (CTAs) as a way to trim the high costs of their dealing rooms, a senior banker said.
"The true costs of bank dealers are greatly understated," said Jerome Raffaldini, president and chief executive officer of Nippon Credit Asset Management Inc, a unit of Nippon Credit Bank Ltd.
Speaking at a Managed Account Report conference, he said cost was not the only issue in using outside CTAs' managed futures. The portfolios of typical dealing rooms are often poorly managed, he said.

Dealers often trade with similar methodology and are influenced by a senior dealer, causing a lack of diversity, he said. Allocation of capital among them is subjective and measuring their performance is difficult, he added.
Using managed futures with diverse trading vehicles and methodologies can achieve a substantially lower volatility in performance, Raffaldini said.
The job of bankers would be to ensure that the CTAs' trading methods stay consistent and to periodically rebalance fund allocation.

The problem, Raffaldini said, was that people in dealing rooms would not welcome such a move. Also, senior management might not be familiar with the concept of managed futures investment, where lower returns must sometimes be tolerated for the sake of stable performance.
Nonetheless, Raffaldini said CTAs were "superior" to traditional bank dealers, citing their competitive fee structure and more disciplined trading methods.
"Bank dealers' salaries do not go down, they go up. In good years, they go up a lot," he said, adding that the cost of supporting a dealing room capable of producing the same diversity was enormous.

Asked if there was a trend among banks to shift their proprietary trading to managed futures, Raffaldini said: "It's a logical thing to do for banks. I think banks will be very powerful players in the industry."
He predicted that banks could be the biggest participants in managed futures in three or four years.

However, Lemuel Seabrook, vice president of treasury at Bank of Montreal, said managed futures would complement, not replace, bank dealing rooms as banks seek expertise in foreign securities or commodities.
"I don't think it will supplant internal dealing rooms, but it's a good way of diversifying," he told Reuters after the conference. -Derivatives Desk 312-408-8750 E-mail: derivatives@reuters.com
